summary: This program defines a RobotPet class whose battery level is guarded by a property, so the value can never fall below 0 or rise above 100. It then walks and charges a pet named Rover, checking first whether it has enough energy for each walk.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery here does not create a plain attribute; it runs the setter defined below, so even a value passed into the constructor gets validated.
The @property decorator turns the method that follows into a read-only attribute, so callers write pet.battery rather than pet.battery().
The real value lives in _battery, and the leading underscore is the convention for "internal, do not touch from outside."
This registers the next method as the code that runs whenever anything assigns to battery, which is what makes the clamping unavoidable.
A walk that drains more than the pet has would produce a negative number, so anything below zero is stored as zero instead.
Charging past a full battery is meaningless, so the value is capped at 100.
The cost of a walk is derived from its length, keeping the rule in one place rather than scattered through the program.
This returns True or False rather than doing anything, letting the caller decide what to do about a low battery.
Subtracting from self.battery sends the result back through the setter, so the level stays in range even if the arithmetic goes negative.
Creating an object calls __init__ with these three values, and the battery of 85 passes validation unchanged.
A ten-minute walk costs 20%, which Rover can afford, so this run exercises the successful branch.
Asking before acting is the point of can_walk: the check and the action are separate methods.
Fifty minutes would cost 100%, more than Rover's remaining 65%, so this run exercises the refusal branch.
Adding 40 to 65 gives 105, and the setter quietly reduces it to 100, demonstrating the validation from the outside.
